newsitem.title: USA: Arctic cold stretches south in U.S. to Texas.
newsitem.headline: Arctic cold stretches south in U.S. to Texas.

text.p: A severe winter storm engulfed the northern U.S. plains on Tuesday, paralysing traffic, closing schools and stranding thousands in their homes amid white-out conditions and bitter cold temperatures.

Snowdrifts as deep as four feet (1.2 metres) closed major highways on Monday in the Dakotas, and authorities said many roads may not be reopened until Wednesday because ploughs have been unable to keep up with the drifts.

Rick Robinson, supervisor of radio communications in North Dakota, said dozens of vehicles were stranded along Interstate-94 and other highways but no snowplows or wreckers were going out in the blizzard on Tuesday.
Weather was blamed for an 18-vehicle pileup in northwest Nebraska. Authorities said no serious injuries were reported in the chain-reaction crash, which happened in zero-visibility on Monday night.
Meteorologists said the temperature Tuesday afternoon was nine degrees (minus 12 celsius) in Minneapolis and in the single digits across the Dakotas.

Todd Heitkamp, meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Sioux Falls, S.D., said rural areas of South Dakota, Minnesota and northwest Iowa were among the worst-hit by the storm on Tuesday. "The wind chills are the real problem. We're going to see the temperature with the wind chill get to 35 to 50 below zero (minus 37 to minus 45 celsius)" Heitkamp said.

Norm Krueger, a spokesman for the North Dakota Division of Emergency Management, said the storm had begun to move out of western areas of the state and visibility was returning. He said that although the storm had not caused any casualties, the severe weather was not yet over. "The winds are ferocious -- gusts of 40 to 50 miles per hour (64 kph to 80 kph)," Krueger said.
Before the storm system left the region on Tuesday night, forecasters said North Dakota would have received another four inches (10 cm) of snow.

In the Black Hills of South Dakota, the added snowfall was putting a new strain on some cities' snow removal budgets. Ted Vore, public works director in Spearfish, S.D., said he had to add $20,000 to his budget to help clear the latest snow.

Driving conditions in Denver caused headaches for commuters on Tuesday morning when heavier-than-expected snowfall on Monday and overnight freezing conditions turned major roads and side streets into sheets of ice.

As the cold temperatures stretched south, homeless shelters in normally warm San Antonio, Tex., were preparing to deal with an onslaught of people seeking to get out of their usual sleeping places in cars and under bridges. Temperatures in San Antonio were expected to dip into the teens.
